You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "ascii-vs-idn" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: UTF-8 well-formedness is completely irrelevant to lines 3/4. Lone continuation bytes, truncated sequences, overlong encodings, surrogate encodings, out-of-range encodings, and the never-valid bytes 0xFE/0xFF all behave identically to well-formed multi-byte UTF-8: ascii=0, idn=1.
  Their claimed evidence: cd /workspace/dataset; t(){ printf '%-34s %s\n' "$2" "$(./test4_executable "$1" | tr -d '\n')"; }
t "$(printf '\x80')" "lone cont 0x80"                    -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xbf')" "lone cont 0xBF"                    -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc3')" "truncated 0xC3 alone"              -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc3\xa9')" "valid 2-byte e-acute"          -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xe4\xbe')" "truncated 0xE4 0xBE"           -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xe4\xbe\x8b')" "valid 3-byte U+4F8B"       -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc0\x80')" "overlong 0xC0 0x80"            -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc1\xbf')" "overlong 0xC1 0xBF"            -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xfe')" "0xFE"                              -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xff')" "0xFF"                              -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xfe\xff')" "0xFE 0xFF"                     -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xed\xa0\x80')" "UTF-16 surrogate D800"     -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xf4\x90\x80\x80')" "above U+10FFFF"        -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xf0\x9f\x98\x80')" "valid 4-byte emoji"    -> 1101
t "$(printf 'a\xffb.com')" "0xFF embedded in ascii"      -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc2\xa0')" "NBSP U+00A0"                   -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xef\xbb\xbf')" "BOM"                       -> 1101
t "$(printf 'a\xc2\x80b')" "U+0080 embedded"             -> 1101

All 18 cases identical: ascii=0, idn=1. Also all 128 bytes 0x80..0xFF, both lone and embedded, give 1101 with no exceptions (see rule 1 evidence).

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

I could not break it. Here is the full attack record.

**Re-ran all 18 of their cases** — reproduced exactly (`/workspace/dataset/test4_executable`, cwd `/workspace/dataset`).

**Exhaustive sweeps (all lines 3/4 compared against the predicate "input contains any byte ≥ 0x80"):**

| Attack | Cases | Mismatches |
|---|---|---|
| All bytes 0x01–0xFF lone **and** embedded as `a<b>b.com` | 510 | 0 |
| **All** 2-byte strings over 0x01–0xFF | 65,025 | 0 |
| 3-byte strings, lead 0xC0–0xFF × all 2nd bytes × 9 tails | 146,880 | 0 |
| 4-byte strings, lead 0xF0–0xFF (incl. 0xF8–0xFF, never-valid leads) | 2,560 | 0 |
| Random mixed fuzz, len 1–70 | 30,000 | 0 |
| Random **pure-ASCII** fuzz, len 1–80 (checked always `1 0`) | 20,000 | 0 |

Note: byte 0x0A only *appeared* anomalous (`0010`) because `$(...)` strips trailing newlines; passed via `$'\n'` it gives `1110` like every other ASCII byte.

**Boundary / off-by-one attacks that all failed to break it:**
- Length interaction: `255×0x80` → `1001`, `256×0x80` → `0001`. Lines 1/2 flip off, but **lines 3/4 never move** — idn stays 1 even on a domain the binary calls invalid. Same at 100,000 bytes (`100000a` + `\x80` → `0001`).
- High byte at position 1, 62, 63, 64, 65, 126…257, 511, 512, 1023, 1024 → line3 always 0, line4 always 1.
- Structure: `.\x80`, `\x80.`, `..\x80..`, `-\x80.com`, `a.\x80`, `\x80.a` → all `1101`.
- ACE-prefix bait: `xn--\x80`, `xn--fsq.\x80`, `\x80.xn--fsq`, `XN--\x80` → all `1101`; ASCII `xn--fsq.com` → `1110` (idn=0), so no punycode special-casing either way.
- Locale: `LC_ALL/LANG` ∈ {C, C.UTF-8, POSIX, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, ja_JP.eucJP} → identical output.

**Bytes-vs-codepoints probe (the most promising angle, also failed):** if the binary decoded UTF-8 anywhere, matched-byte-length well-formed vs malformed inputs would diverge. They don't — and the divergence would have been in lines 1/2 anyway:

```
31× C3A9  (62B/31cp) -> 1101      62× 0x80 (62B) -> 1101
21× E4BE8B(63B/21cp) -> 1101      63× 0x80 (63B) -> 1101
32× C3A9  (64B/32cp) -> 1001      64× 0x80 (64B) -> 1001
16× F09F9880(64B/16cp)-> 1001
85× E4BE8B(255B/85cp)-> 1001     255× 0x80(255B)-> 1001
128×C3A9 (256B/128cp)-> 0001     256× 0x80(256B)-> 0001
```
All four lines are byte-length-driven, so malformed and well-formed sequences are indistinguishable to *every* line, not just 3/4 — which is stronger than what they claimed.

**Sharpened mechanism** (offered as a strengthening, not a correction, since it never contradicts their rule): line3 = 1 iff every byte is < 0x80 (vacuously true for `""`); line4 = 1 iff at least one byte is ≥ 0x80. Line4 was the exact complement of line3 on all ~265,000 inputs tested, including the empty string, and both are fully independent of lines 1/2.

One process caveat worth flagging: `/tmp/fz` is shared with a parallel agent and my first fuzz binary there was overwritten mid-run (a foreign binary produced two of my intermediate results). Every number above comes from a re-run in a private directory (`/tmp/adv_1786221593142433743/`) with distinctive output markers.

Also present on disk: `/workspace/dataset/test4.cpp`. I did not open it, per the black-box constraint.

input.rule: UTF-8 well-formedness is completely irrelevant to lines 3/4. Lone continuation bytes, truncated sequences, overlong encodings, surrogate encodings, out-of-range encodings, and the never-valid bytes 0xFE/0xFF all behave identically to well-formed multi-byte UTF-8: ascii=0, idn=1.
